title: The Foundations of Polycrisis Resilience
subtitle: Defining Resilience in an Era of Interconnected Global Risks
description: A foundational publication establishing that humanity's capacity to withstand interconnected global risks depends not only on responding to individual crises…
contribution: Defines the conceptual foundations of Polycrisis Resilience—originated by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics—advancing the core thesis and three central arguments that vulnerability is interconnected, development is a mechanism of resilience, and resilience must be systemic and preventative.
abstract:
The Foundations of Polycrisis Resilience serves as a foundational conceptual publication within the H Heuristics Polycrisis Resilience Series, based on the concept developed by Hunter Hughes, Founder of H Heuristics (https://polycrisisresilience.hheuristics.com/).
It defines resilience in an era of interconnected global risks, advancing the central thesis that improving humanity's long-term resilience requires improving the underlying conditions of human development and systemic stability through sustainable development, economic convergence, technological diffusion, climate adaptation, environmental improvement, and institutional strengthening.

keyFindings.title: Humanity's capacity to withstand interconnected global risks depends not only on responding to individual crises, but on systematically reducing the underlying human and systemic vulnerabilities that allow those risks to emerge, compound, and propagate.

Vulnerability is interconnected: economic deprivation, environmental degradation, inadequate infrastructure, technological exclusion, institutional weaknesses, and climate exposure reinforce one another, amplifying a 16.0% primary climate shock into a 58.0% compounded systemic loss.

Development is a mechanism of resilience: improvements in living standards, infrastructure, public health, energy systems, education, technology access, and institutional capacity reduce vulnerability across multiple risk dimensions simultaneously.
Resilience must be systemic and preventative: ex-ante structural investments deliver 6.8x–11.4x social benefit-cost ratios compared with 1.3x–1.7x for reactive crisis relief and bailouts.
